examples.title: Halfway House
examples.lesson: A long gap with one small crimp halfway: reach past it, or hang on it.
text: Between the start jugs and the next jug J1 there is a long gap. The only thing in it is a small crimp, C, off to the side, and there are no footholds between the floor and the high ones.

{B.label} is tall enough to reach J1 straight from the start, with the feet still low (crux {B.crux}). {A.label} is not: she pulls onto the crimp with both hands, steps her feet up to the high footholds, and reaches J1 from there. It works, but at her limit (crux {A.crux}).

{C.label} gets a hand onto the crimp but is {C.fail}. With one hand on a crimp and both feet to one side, the body needs a little grip twist to stay square, and a weak grip on a small edge cannot give it: a barn-door.
{D.label} cannot use the crimp at all ({D.fail}), and without it J1 is out of reach.

checks.text: Ava uses the crimp before she reaches J1
Ben's first hand move goes straight to J1
Cal gets onto the crimp before failing
Ava (injured) is stopped by the crimp itself

examples.title: Fork in the Road
examples.lesson: Small crimps straight up, or big jugs far out to the right.
text: Two ways up. On the left, three small crimps in a line, with every foothold a few centimetres to their right. On the right, two big jugs, J1 and J2, so far apart that only a long reach links them.
{A.label} takes the crimps (crux {A.crux}). With every foothold off to one side, a hand on a crimp has to twist a little to keep the body square, and her strong fingers can.
{B.label} takes the jugs (crux {B.crux}), using a crimp only as a step while the other hand is on a jug, which does the twisting.
{C.label} is {C.fail}. The same twist is too much for a weaker grip, and the body swings open.
{D.label} is {D.fail}. She has Ava's body, so her failure also shows that the jugs alone are too far apart for a climber of Ava's size.

checks.text: Ava climbs on the crimps and never touches the jugs
Cal fails by a barn-door (direction or balance)
Ava (injured) is stopped by a crimp

examples.title: Lean on Me
examples.lesson: A layback: hands pull sideways on a flake, feet push back, and nothing may twist open.
text: A flake runs straight up: four sidepulls, L1 to L4, that pull the hands to the right, with the footholds almost directly below them, a few centimetres to the right. The hands pull, the feet push back, and every time a hand or foot moves, whatever stays on must also stop the body twisting open.

{B.label} gets up too (crux {B.crux}), but needs {B.steps} moves, with more shuffling. He stands further from the wall, so his hands must pull in harder, and the same small offset of the feet needs more twist.

{C.label} gets both hands onto L2 and then cannot move either foot: one foot pushing a few centimetres to the side of two weak sidepull grips swings the body open. With the feet stuck low, Cal is {C.fail}.
{D.label} climbs exactly like Ava (crux {D.crux}): a sidepull is held like a pinch, so her injured finger does not matter here.

checks.text: Ava's and Ava (injured)'s betas are the same
Ben needs more moves than Ava
Cal is stuck with both hands on L2 and his feet low
